title: In command: what it means to lead a business without being "in control"
summary: Jason Cohen argues that control is impossible but command is achievable. A leader who is in command still has bugs, missed metrics, mistakes and threats. What sets her apart is that she has expectations, watches the right metrics, writes down her thinking, and reacts honestly when reality diverges. The essay lists what command looks like across metrics, hiring, strategy, sales, backlog and decisions.

principles.text: Being in command means having expectations and reacting when you miss them, not always meeting them.
principles.quote: It means you *have* expectations of yourself and your team, and when you don't meet them, it bothers you, and you react.

principles.text: Decide which few metrics matter up front, so you spot problems first and respond in proportion to their importance.
principles.quote: When metrics go awry, you're the first one to identify that, and are already taking action in proportion to their importance and how far off the mark they are.

principles.text: A long backlog is fine if you pick a few strategic bets and have a system for prioritizing, which means doing almost none of the rest.
principles.quote: It means you've identified the few Rocks that are your bets on how to win strategically, and you have a system for prioritizing the rest, which also means doing almost none of the rest.

principles.text: If you constantly do others' work, it's your fault: you hired wrong or won't let good hires do their job. Edit rather than write.
principles.quote: If you're constantly having to do someone else's work, that's your fault. Either you've hired incorrectly, which is your fault, or you have hired correctly and you're not allowing them to do their job, which is your fault.

principles.text: Write down what you believe so you can tell when your mind needs to change, then communicate what changed and why.
principles.quote: It means you wrote down what you think, so that it's more obvious when your mind needs to change, and then you communicate that change--both what and why.

principles.text: Seek out surprises and hard truths. Surprises should come from new facts, never from negligence.
principles.quote: It means when they do occur, it's not due to negligence. It means something actually changed, or an important new fact was uncovered.
